Rebels, and those who serve idols.
These are criminals (*avraynim*) who transgress other prohibitions.
An expression of *elah*, a kind of tree, which is called *olme* in Old French.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is אולמ״א; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Les ormes”) and reads *olme* (modern *orme*, elm).

Isaiah.english_translation: To worship idols beneath them, as is said (Hosea 4:13): “under oaks and poplars and terebinths, because the shadow thereof is good.”
There they worshipped idols, as you say: “They that sanctify themselves and purify themselves to go unto the gardens” (below 66:17).

Its leaf withers, fades, *flatissant* in Old French; when a scorching wind or frost comes upon it, it withers and its moisture is lost and gone. And *novel* is not an expression of rot, like *balah*, for the *nun* does not occur in that language; rather, *novel* is an expression of a thing that is weary and spent, as from the root *naval*, “thou wilt surely wear away” (*navol tibol*) (Exodus 18:18), like *tinbol*; and we translate it *mil'ah tilah*.
Isaiah.translator_note:
Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is פלישטיישנ״ט; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse and reads *flatisant* (“Se flétrissant”).
u|The grammatical explanation is terse; translated literally.

Isaiah.english_translation: To water its seeds; with the thing through which they sin, He makes their punishment equal.

The mighty one, who used to force the poor and rob them and strengthen himself (*mitchasnim*) with money, as he said above: “and companions of thieves”; that money will be as tow (*ne'oret*), which is shaken (*mena'arin*) from flax, which is light and easy to burn.

And the one who makes it strong will be a spark of fire, and they will burn each other. Spark: *estencele* in Old French. Targum Jonathan: *u-fo'ulo* (“and the work of their hands”); and this is not according to the Hebrew language, for then he should have pointed *u-fa'alo* with a *chataf kamatz* and it would be explained as an expression of *pa'al*; now that it is pointed with a *cholam*, it is explained as an expression of *po'el*.
Isaiah.translator_note:
Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is אישטנציל״א; Darmesteter (1909) reads *éstencéle* (modern *étincelle*).
u|The grammatical remark at the end is terse in the printed text; translated literally.

Isaiah.english_translation: Targum Jonathan: *ve-la yehe aleihon chayis* (“and there shall be none upon them who has pity”).
Isaiah.translator_note: The Aramaic is transliterated, with a literal gloss. The site’s JPS verse ends before “And none shall quench them”, so the bold lemma is taken from the preceding words.

Isaiah.english_translation: After the transgressors have ended.
Prepared.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: as the top of the mountains
Isaiah.english_translation: On the mountain that is the head of all the mountains in the importance of mountains.
It will be great, a miracle that will be done on it of the miracles of Sinai and Carmel and Tabor.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: all nations shall flow unto it
Isaiah.english_translation: They shall gather; they shall be drawn to it like rivers.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: To the house of the God of Jacob
Isaiah.english_translation: Because he called it Beth-el, therefore it will be called by his name; but Abraham called it “in the mount of the LORD it shall be seen”; Isaac called it “field,” “to meditate in the field.”
*Coltres* in Old French.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is קולטר״ש; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Coutres”) and reads *coltres*.

Isaiah.english_translation: *Serpes* in Old French, with which they prune vineyards.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is שרפ״ש; Darmesteter (1909) reads *serpes* (“Serpes”).

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: O house of Jacob, come you
Isaiah.english_translation: The nations will say to them so; and this verse refers back to “And many peoples shall go,” etc.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: In the light of the LORD
Isaiah.english_translation: They will say to them so; and Jonathan translated: *yeimrun de-veit Ya'akov atu*, etc. (“they will say: House of Jacob, come”).

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: For Thou hast forsaken Thy people the house of Jacob
Isaiah.english_translation: The prophet turns the speech to the Shekhinah and says: for until now You have forsaken Your people because of their iniquity. (Another: The prophet rebukes them and says to them thus, “for Thou hast forsaken Thy people the house of Jacob,” etc.: you have forsaken the good deed through which you became a people — a man — you, house of Jacob.)
Isaiah.translator_note: The parenthetical alternative is terse in the printed text; translated literally.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: For they are replenished from the east
Isaiah.english_translation: Their hosts were filled with the deeds of Arameans who lived in the east, who were sorcerers and made use of the name of idolatry.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: And they please themselves in the brood of aliens
Isaiah.english_translation: They cohabit with the daughters of idolaters and mingle with them, and they bear them children, and with them they constantly occupy themselves, and embrace them, and trouble themselves with them: an expression of “lest He entice thee with *sefek*” (Job 36:18): *debatement* in Old French.
Isaiah.translator_note:
Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is דביטימנ״ט; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse with variants such as *debatement* and glosses it “Action de se battre” (the attribution of that gloss to this entry is not certain from my copy).
The quotation from Job 36:18 is left with the Hebrew word *sefek* untranslated (JPS renders the verse differently).

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: Neither is there any end of their treasures
Isaiah.english_translation: An expression of *ketz* (end).
Like *mishtachavim*.
The small ones.
The great and the mighty, men of valour.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: And Thou canst not bear with them
Isaiah.english_translation: The prophet says to the Holy One, blessed be He: And I know that You will not forgive them from exacting punishment of them.
To enter into a rock, to flee into the clefts of the rocks.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: And hide thee in the dust
Isaiah.english_translation: And to be hidden in the dust.
Haughtiness of spirit, and so every expression of lofty eyes in Scripture, as you say (Psalms 101:5): “haughty of eye and proud of heart.”
It is an example for the mighty.
The rulers, since oaks are lesser than cedars.
Upon their inhabitants.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: And upon all the ships of Tarshish
Isaiah.english_translation: Jonathan translated: *ve-al kol deyatvin be-nisei yama* (“and upon all who dwell in the … of the sea”), in the islands of the sea, whose goods are found and brought by ships.
Isaiah.translator_note: The Targum phrase *nisei yama* is left in transliteration because its sense is unclear in the printed text.

Isaiah.english_translation: The name of a sea whose name is Tarshish.
Palaces paved with *maskiyot* of marble flooring, like “and a figured stone” (*even maskit*) (Leviticus 26:1), named so because they cover the ground with it.
It is the Day of Judgment.
It will pass away entirely; all of them will perish.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: And men shall go into the caves of the rocks
Isaiah.english_translation: The inhabitants of the earth into the caves of rocks.
They are caves.
For the Day of Judgment.
To break the wicked of the earth.
Idols in the likeness of *chafarperot*, kinds of creeping things that dig the ground, which are called *talpes* in Old French.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is טלפ״ש; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Aux taupes”) and reads *talpes* (modern *taupes*).

Isaiah.english_translation: *Calve-sorriz* in Old French. One can also interpret: his idols that he made for himself to worship, a man will cast into the crevices and the holes that he finds before him as he goes to flee and hide.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is קלבא שורי״ץ; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Les chauves-souris”) and reads *calve-sorriz*.

Isaiah.english_translation: From listening to those who lead you astray from after Me and to bow down to the work of his hands.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: in whose nostrils is a breath
Isaiah.english_translation: Whose whole life and strength depend on the breath of his nostrils, which is a flying wind: today it is in him and tomorrow it departs from him; and all the more so the likeness of moles, which has no substance. Another interpretation: Cease from all evil ways and learn from man in whose nostrils is breath: have you seen of what account he is? And all the more so (the idols) that are not accounted as anything.
Isaiah.translator_note: The word “(the idols)” is a parenthetical addition in the printed Hebrew.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: Doth take away from Jerusalem and from Judah
Isaiah.english_translation: It is all explained in tractate Chagigah: Isaiah cursed Israel with eighteen curses, and his mind was not cooled until he said (below, verse 5): “The child shall behave insolently against the aged, and the base against the honourable.”
This is a king, as it is said (Proverbs 16:10): “A divine sentence is in the lips of the king.”
One who knows how to intercalate years and to fix months.
For when he opens with words of Torah, all become as if deaf (*cheresh*).
Fit to be entrusted with the secrets of the Torah, which were given in a whisper (*lachash*), such as the Account of Creation and the Account of the Chariot.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: I will give children to be their princes
Isaiah.english_translation: These are people who are shaken free (*menu'arim*) of the commandments.

*Ta'alulim*: *shu'alim* [as printed], weak people; and I say, according to its plain sense, *ta'alulim* are scoffers among men, who make sport of them and shame them, like “and I have *olalti* my horn in the dust” (Job, chapter 15 [as printed]); “that I have *hit'allalti*” (Exodus 10).
Isaiah.translator_note: The printed word שועלים is unclear and is left in transliteration. The printed reference “Job 15” appears to be Job 16:15 (JPS: “have laid my horn in the dust”); JPS renders the Exodus 10:2 verb as “wrought”.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: the people shall oppress one another
Isaiah.english_translation: They will be pressed and oppressed one upon another in *tigur* and *chirum*.
Isaiah.translator_note: The Hebrew words *tigur* and *chirum* are left in transliteration; their sense here is unclear.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: The child shall behave insolently against the aged
Isaiah.english_translation: The child will grow great over the elder.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: And the base against the honourable
Isaiah.english_translation: According to its plain sense; and its Midrash: one will come to whom serious matters seem like light ones, and will be insolent against one to whom light matters seem like serious ones.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: For a man shall take hold of his brother of the house of his father
Isaiah.english_translation: When a man takes hold of his brother in his father’s house, saying: You are rich in Torah, and it is clear in your hand like a garment.
And teach us.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: And let this ruin be under thy hand
Isaiah.english_translation: That we stumble in it, in prohibition or in permission, in uncleanness or in cleanness, is under your hand, for you know how to instruct us. Another interpretation: a garment is for you, to clothe the naked.

(*Faylance* in Old French) from my lack, as I am lacking bread, is under your hand to supply me; and therefore “be thou our ruler.” And he answers: In my house there is no bread and no mantle; and what is my worth as a ruler?
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is פיילנצ״א; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Faiblesse”) and reads *faylience* (*faillance*).

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: In that day shall he swear
Isaiah.english_translation: *Yissa* is nothing but an expression of an oath. He will swear to them: I will not be a *chovesh*, I will not be of the bandagers (*chovshim*) of the house of study; and in my house there is no bread and mantle; I have in my hand neither a reason of Mishnah nor a reason of Aggadah. Another interpretation, according to its plain sense: I will not be a *chovesh*, I will not be a judge, who imprisons (*chovesh*) the condemned in the prison.
All of them are lacking and fallen, and none helps the other; and why? because they refused to listen, and now all of them provoke.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: Because their tongue and their doings are against the LORD
Isaiah.english_translation: Opposite Him, to provoke Him.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: To provoke the eyes of His glory
Isaiah.english_translation: To vex before His glory. Another interpretation: the matters (*inyanei*) of His glory.
The iniquity that they show partiality in judgment testifies against them before Me. Another version: The recognition of their faces — they are recognized by the impudence of their faces.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: And they declare their sin as Sodom
Isaiah.english_translation: They did not conceal; they did it publicly.
To him who is righteous: that he has done good.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: Woe unto the wicked! it shall be ill with him
Isaiah.english_translation: Who is evil to himself and evil to others; he causes evil to himself and to others; in Tanchuma. And the verse refers back to “Say you of the righteous, that it shall be well with him,” and “Woe unto the wicked! it shall be ill with him.”
They are scoffers.

Adulterous women rule over them, as he says below: “because the daughters of Zion are haughty and have turned their heart to evil” (therefore all the weak ones rule over him); and Jonathan translated the language of (creditors, *noshim*).
Isaiah.translator_note: The quotation from “below” (Isaiah 3:16) does not match the verse’s wording as printed (the second half is not in the verse); both parentheticals appear to be later additions.

Isaiah.english_translation: Your guides, who have to direct you in the good way, they cause them to err.
They corrupted.
Of Israel, standing, so as not to be exacting in their judgment.
And He delays and prolongs in the judgment of the nations. This “standing” is an expression of delay.
For they should have protested; and to the idolaters He says: “You have consumed My vineyard; I was angry a little, and you helped for evil.”

A generation that was poor in good deeds. All this is in Midrash Aggadah; and according to the plain meaning, the entire matter is about Israel, and “and standeth to judge the peoples” — they are the tribes.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: It is you that have eaten up the vineyard
Isaiah.english_translation: The elders and the princes consumed the rest of the people.
*Malachem* — like *mah lachem*.
Crush and diminish, to shame them in their judgment.
About the women who ruled over My people: “because they are haughty,” etc.
An expression of looking. Another interpretation: they paint their eyes with *sikra* (red dye) and with kohl.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: Walking and mincing as they go
Isaiah.english_translation: An expression of something floating on top of its fellow, like (Deuteronomy 11) “made to overflow,” and we translate *de-atif*: when a tall woman walked between two short ones, so that she would appear to float above them. And Jonathan translated: *u-fatehan mekafan*. They used to tie on foreign locks, braiding detached hairs and wrapping them together with their own braids, so that they would look thick and plump (*tefufot*).

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: making a tinkling with their feet
Isaiah.english_translation: When they passed in the marketplace beside the young men of Israel, she would tread on his foot with hers and hint to him in the manner of an adulteress’s love, in order to kindle the evil inclination in him — like this *ekes* of a snake. *Ekes* is the venom of a snake.

An expression of leprosy (*tzara'at*), like (Leviticus 13) “it is a *mispachat*”; and because it is written with a *sin* (*shin*), our Rabbis expounded it to mean that they will become *shifchot mekhudanot*; and some expounded that many families of lice would come upon them. *Pothen ye'areh* — *kleihen ye'areh*. It is an Aramaic expression: it is *pitya ukhma*. They used to say: “Let Him make speed, let Him hasten His work” — a prince will see me and take me. When the calamity came, the princes of Nebuchadnezzar took them to be wives because of their beauty, and the Holy One, blessed be He, hinted: and they were flowing, like a man who pours from vessel to vessel; and as they were punished with menstrual blood, they became loathsome to them, and they cast them to the ground from their carriages. And Targum Jonathan: *yekarhen ye'adei* (“their glory He will remove”).
Isaiah.translator_note: The explanation is terse and partly obscure in the printed text; the words *shifchot mekhudanot*, *pothen ye'areh*, *kleihen ye'areh* and *pitya ukhma* are left in transliteration. The words “Let Him make speed, let Him hasten His work” are the wording of Isaiah 5:19.

Isaiah.english_translation: *Pothen* — an expression of width, an expression of greatness.

In the future to come, when the Holy One, blessed be He, comes to return Israel to Him, “the LORD will remove from them the glory of the anklets,” so that they will no longer hang their glory on the beauty of women’s ornaments and matters of obscenity.
The shoes that are on their feet, with which they “make a tinkling.”
Kinds of net (*sevakhah*) for head ornaments; and there is much of it in the language of the Mishnah: a *shavis* of a net.
Jonathan translated: *ve-sivkhaya*.

*Onkaya*, an expression of “chains about thy neck” (Proverbs 1:9); and the expression *netifot* is named for the fact that they hang on the neck and drip (*notfot*) on the breast; and they are a kind of pearl, perforated and strung on a thread; and in Old French, *mostences*.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is מושטינצא״ש; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Des colliers”) with manuscript forms such as *mostners*; I give a Frenchified transliteration of the printed form, which is not matched exactly.

Isaiah.english_translation: Bracelets of the arm, which are translated *ve-shirya*.

A wrap with which they wrap all their faces except the eyeball, so that a man will desire to be nourished by looking at the cheeks (*sa''a*). Another interpretation: *ha-ra'alot* are kinds of fine cloaks for wrapping oneself, and in the language of the Mishnah there are *madiyot re'ulot* in tractate Shabbat.
Isaiah.translator_note: The abbreviation סא״א in the printed text looks like a later insertion.

Isaiah.english_translation: Targum: *kelilaya*, like (Exodus 39) “the *pa'arei* of the caps.”
An anklet of the shins.
As it sounds: binders — short ones with which they bind their hair; and some make them gilded; *freis* in Old French.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is פרשיינ״ש; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Des ceintures”) with forms such as *orfrés*, *frays*, *froys* (all the same sense); my transliteration of the printed form is approximate.

Isaiah.english_translation: What is opposite the heart; *nosche* in Old French.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is נושק״א; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Des sachets”) and reads *nosches* (which in Old French generally has the sense of bracelets).

Isaiah.english_translation: Ear-rings; the place where one whispers (*lochashin*) to her.
*Kitunaya* (tunics), like (II Samuel 2) “and take their *chalitzatam*” — that the body is clothed in them, and when they take them off they remove (*chol'tzin*) them from the body.
Isaiah.translator_note: The printed quotation reads *chalitzatam*; the verse (2 Samuel 2:21) reads “take thee his armour” (*chalitzato*).

Isaiah.english_translation: Bed-coverings, as its Targum: *shushipaya*. “And the *mitpachot*” — tablecloths.
Its Targum is *machkaya*, a mould of the womb, as we translate “and *kumaz*” (Exodus 35): *machoch*.
Isaiah.translator_note: The comparison with the Targum of Exodus 35 is translated literally and not checked.

Isaiah.english_translation: They are the mirrors, as its Targum: *machzayata* (*espekiu* in Old French); because they reveal (*megalin*) the shapes of the faces they are called *giluyonim*, or perhaps their mirrors used to be rolled up (*nigl'lot*).
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is ספייקיי״ו; I did not match it in Darmesteter (his entry for this verse, “Des miroirs”, reads *miradoyr*, a different word). My transliteration is of the printed form only.

Isaiah.english_translation: On linen — they are those in which one wraps oneself.
(*Molekins* in Old French.)
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is מולקינ״ש; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Des moquettes”) and reads *molekin*. The parenthesis looks like a later addition.

Isaiah.english_translation: *Kevinta* (*fermalz* in Old French), and they are of gold, with which they fasten the cloak in which the woman wraps herself.
Isaiah.translator_note:
Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is פרמל״ץ; Darmesteter (1909) reads *fermalz* (*fermail*).
u|The verb *mechavnin* is rendered “fasten”; its sense is not certain.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: sweet spices there shall be rottenness
Isaiah.english_translation: The place where they perfumed themselves will be rotten (*nimak*).

The place where she girded herself will be *nikaf* — cut with wounds and marks of blows — like “and after my skin they have *nikfu*” (Job 19) and “and He shall cut down (*venikaf*) the thickets of the forest” (below, 10).
Isaiah.translator_note: The verse in Job 19:26 reads “And when after my skin this is destroyed”; Rashi takes the verb to mean “cut.”

Isaiah.english_translation: The place where they used to do the deed mentioned above, “walking and mincing as they go,” which is at the height of the head — there will be *mikshah*, baldness; a blow that makes the head bald. *Mikshah* is an expression of “this to that *nakshan*” (Daniel 5). And I used to explain it: “instead of the work of *mikshah*” — the place where the girdles set the plates of gold made of one piece (*mikshah*), *batedic* in Old French — except that it is pointed with a *patach*, and in the Masorah it is among ten that are pointed with a *patach*, none of which is attached to the word after it; and every *ma'aseh* attached to the word after it is pointed with a *kamatz*.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is בטדי״ץ; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Frappé au marteau”) and reads *batedic*.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: instead of a stomacher a girding of sackcloth
Isaiah.english_translation: And it is (another version: “behold”) like two words, *pati gil*: a vessel that brings them to joy (*gilah*); and it is the womb mentioned above — *pothen*; in exchange for that joy there will be a girding of sackcloth on all her loins.
Isaiah.translator_note: The explanation is terse in the printed text.

Isaiah.english_translation: For this is fitting to be for them instead of the beauty in which they took pride.
Your mighty men — the men of your wars, who go out in the army by number.
An expression of mourning (*aninah*).
The gates of towns and houses: in all her gates there will be lamentation.
And she will be emptied of everything, like “And I also have given you cleanness of teeth” (Amos 4); and in the language of the Mishnah: “So-and-so went out clean of his property.”

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: she shall sit upon the ground
Isaiah.english_translation: From height to lowliness: “They sit upon the ground, and keep silence” (Lamentations 2) on the Ninth of Av.
And they will grasp.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: seven women shall take hold of one man
Isaiah.english_translation: Because of the many widows, they ask one man that he marry them.

Hide our reproach, like “then thou shalt bring it home to thy house” (Deuteronomy 21 [as printed]), for when a woman is married, one does not treat her as ownerless. Another interpretation: Nebuchadnezzar decreed that they not cohabit with … so that they not be punished; therefore they asked that his name be called upon them.
Isaiah.translator_note:
The printed reference “Deuteronomy 21:12” does not match the quotation “*ve-asafto el toch beitecha*”, which is Deuteronomy 22:2 (JPS: “then thou shalt bring it home to thy house”).
u|In the second explanation the printed abbreviation א״א is not clear to me and is left untranslated; the opening abbreviation מ״א is read as “another interpretation.”

Isaiah.english_translation: After the beauty of the ornaments of the adulteresses and the lewd women has ended, the glory of the beauty of their honour in these will no longer end (another version: “will no longer be cast aside”).
For you, as beauty.
They are the righteous who remain among them, and the wise, the students of Torah; on them they will hang the glory of their beauty.

They are the children of the righteous, “the fruit of the tree of life”; they will be for pride and for splendour, in which the remnant of Israel will boast and be praised. *Tzvi* — beauty; a thing of desire, which has delight in it.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: he that is left in Zion
Isaiah.english_translation: Among them in Zion they will settle.
In every place they will dwell in Jerusalem.

All of them will be righteous. And if you say that the righteous who died before that day, their honour has been lost — Scripture teaches: “every one that is written unto life,” that is, for the life of the World to Come; they will be in Jerusalem. From the manuscript.

*Im rachatz* — there is an *im* used in the sense of *ki*; and so in the language of *ki*, and so (Job 8:18) “*im yeval'enu mi-mekomo*” — “*ki yeval'enu*”; “until they have done drinking” (Genesis 24:19) [*ad im kilu li-shtot*].
Defilement, as its Targum — that is, He will remove their iniquity through afflictions and through removal from the world.
An expression of washing, in the language of the Mishnah and in Scripture: “and there they rinse the burnt-offering” (Ezekiel 40:38).
Through afflictions; *talent* in Old French — that it come up in His spirit to judge them.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is טלנ״ט; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Un esprit de justice”) and reads *talant* (will, desire).

Isaiah.english_translation: To destroy them from the world. *Ba'ar* is like *le-va'er*; *descombrement* in Old French; an expression of a passive form (*po'ul*), “going.”
Isaiah.translator_note:
Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is דישקומבמ״ט; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Un esprit de destruction”) and reads *déscombrement* (obstruction).
u|The final phrase (ל׳ פעול הלוך) is terse and its sense is not certain.

Isaiah.english_translation: Those called within it.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: a cloud and smoke by day
Isaiah.english_translation: To protect them from the nations.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: for over all the glory shall be a canopy
Isaiah.english_translation: Mentioned for them there will be the canopy, in that My Shekhinah will hover over them. And there are seven canopies here: cloud, smoke, brightness, fire, flame, canopy, Shekhinah.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: a pavilion for a shadow in the day-time from the heat
Isaiah.english_translation: From drought, to protect from the heat of the coming day, as is said of the wicked: “And the day that cometh shall set them ablaze” (Malachi 3); for the Holy One, blessed be He, takes the sun out of its sheath and heats it upon them.
Isaiah.translator_note: The words *mi-chorev* and *u-mekadrah* are not certain in sense.

Isaiah.english_translation: An expression of covering.
To be hidden in it.
Fire that streams from the river of Dinur upon the wicked in Gehinnom, as it is said (Jeremiah 23:19): “It shall whirl upon the head of the wicked” — in tractate Chagigah.
Rain that falls upon the wicked, as in the matter that is said: “*yamter al reshaim pachim*” (Psalms 11:6).
Isaiah.translator_note: JPS renders the verse: “Upon the wicked He will cause to rain coals.”

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: Let me sing of my well-beloved
Isaiah.english_translation: The prophet says: “Let me sing of my beloved” — in place of my beloved, and in his stead, and on his errand, like “The LORD will fight for you” (Exodus 14:14) — on your behalf.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: A song of my beloved touching his vineyard
Isaiah.english_translation: It is this that he sang on behalf of his vineyard, concerning his vineyard, like “and the men of the place asked ... concerning his wife” (Genesis 26:7).
A fat son (*ben shemen*) in corners, producing fat fruits like good oil.
*Zaviyot* — fit for oil, for olives, to make oil, like *ben mavet* (II Samuel 2 [as printed]) — fit to die; and a parallel to this is this, and at the end of the matter he will explain it.
Isaiah.translator_note:
The printed reference “II Samuel 2” does not match; the phrase *ben mavet* is at II Samuel 12:5 (JPS: “deserveth to die”).
u|The first word is attached to the preceding heading in the printed text.

Isaiah.english_translation: He fenced it and walled it around, encircled like a ring, which we translate *izka*.
He removed from within it the stones that are bad for vines, like “clear it of stones” (below 62).
They are the shoots that are better for planting than other shoots.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: built a tower in the midst of it
Isaiah.english_translation: A winepress, for pressing grapes.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: also hewed out a vat therein
Isaiah.english_translation: The pit in front of the winepress to receive the wine; and so every *yekev* in Scripture is an expression of a pit, and so “unto the *yikvei* of the king” (Zechariah 14:10), Targum Jonathan: *ad shichya de-malka* — it is the depth of the ocean; and therefore an expression of hewing falls on it here, like “and cisterns hewn out” (Deuteronomy 6).

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: he looked that it should bring forth grapes
Isaiah.english_translation: And my beloved hoped that this vineyard would make grapes for him.
Resembling grapes, and they call them *lanbruyest* in Old French.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is לנברווייש״ט; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Des lambruches”) and reads *lanbruises* (from *lambrusca*, wild vine).

Isaiah.english_translation: To remove the fence that covers and protects it. *Mesukhah* is a hedge of thorns; *gader* is a fence of stones.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: And it shall be eaten up
Isaiah.english_translation: The vineyard.
So that cattle and beast will graze in it.
An expression of desolation and emptiness, and so (below 7) “*u-ve-nachalei ha-batot*” (“in the rugged valleys”).
It is an expression of the digging of a vineyard.

Kinds of thorns — Menachem ben Saruk interpreted them so; but I say that *shamir* is an expression of a worm, a strong one, which splits stones, with which Solomon built the Temple, as in the matter that is said (Ezekiel 3:9): “As an adamant harder than flint.”

An expression of “desolation and destruction” (Lamentations 3:47); an expression of *tisha*, desolate (below 6). Its side, there being none who seeks to enter it, and from this a worm will come up in it.
Isaiah.translator_note: The phrase “its side” (צדו) is translated literally; its sense here is not certain.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: the vineyard of the LORD of hosts
Isaiah.english_translation: To this vineyard you are likened, house of Israel, for all that He did to this vineyard He did to Israel. And the vineyard is Adam the first, for we find in *M.A.* in many places, in Tanchuma and in Bereshit Rabbah, that these verses are expounded about him: Adam was not driven out until he blasphemed and reviled, as it is said, “And he looked that it should bring forth grapes,” etc.; and in another place we find that He set guards over him so that he not eat of the tree of life, as it is said, “I will also command the clouds”; and so we expounded about him.
Isaiah.translator_note: The printed abbreviation במ״א is left as printed (probably “in Midrash Aggadah”, but not expanded in the text).

Isaiah.english_translation: This is Adam the first.
Isaiah.translator_note: In the printed text a parenthesis opens before this word and closes after ISA.5.7.4 (“In the Garden of Eden”); it appears to mark a Midrashic explanation of verses 1–6.

Isaiah.english_translation: This is the Holy One, blessed be He.
In the Garden of Eden.
With the ten canopies mentioned (in Ezekiel 28) in the section of Hiram king of Tyre.
From the evil inclination, until he ate of the tree and the evil inclination entered into him.
The beginning of his creation was from the place of the altar.
“And breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” — from the upper ones.
A flowing spring, a source of wisdom.
That he would give thanks and praise before Him.
Putrid (*nivashim*) things: he blasphemed and reviled.
Because the end of the parable comes to say that they too did as he did, He asks them for the judgment.
What seems proper in My eyes to do to him — and I did it.
I drove him out from within his canopies.
His end is to die, and for wild beasts to rule over him.
I drove him out from the partition of the Garden of Eden.
His side I caused to cease, for I gave no Torah in his days.
Isaiah.translator_note: The word צדו is translated literally as “his side”; its sense here is not certain.

Isaiah.english_translation: They will not learn from him either merit or good deed.
The evil inclination ruled over him, and over his generations after him, to do corrupt deeds.
I commanded guardians over him to guard the way of the tree of life.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: the vineyard of the LORD of hosts
Isaiah.english_translation: For like that vineyard is the house of Israel to Me — the ten tribes: they were to Me like a vineyard of wine, like a vineyard of olive, like a horn of oil in a land of fatness — the oil of the priesthood, the oil of the kingship, the oil of the Menorah, the oil of the meal-offerings. I fenced them at first with the encircling of the clouds of glory in the wilderness, and I cleared them of stones, and cleansed them of the transgressors of the generation. I planted them with *sorek* — six hundred and six commandments, by the numerical value of *sorek*; I added to them the seven commandments that the sons of Noah were commanded. I built a tower in its midst — My Tabernacle and My Sanctuary; and also a vat — the altar and the foundation pits.
They corrupted their deeds.

Whom I have not yet exiled — let them judge between Me and between them concerning the evil that I brought upon them: who rebelled against whom? What more was there to do for My vineyard that I did not do for it?
You too, who provoke Me — [I will tell you] what is fitting in My eyes to do to My vineyard, like all that I did to Adam the first.
I will remove My Shekhinah from them, which covers them, as it is said (below 52 [as printed]): “And the covering of Judah was laid bare.”
Isaiah.translator_note: The printed reference “below 52” does not match; the words are in Isaiah 22:8 (JPS: “And the covering of Judah was laid bare”).

Isaiah.english_translation: I will tear down its walls.
*Ve-ashvinun reteshin* (Targum Jonathan).
Isaiah.translator_note: The Aramaic is left in transliteration; it is Rashi’s citation of the Targum without introduction.

Isaiah.english_translation: *Lo estaadun ve-lo yistamchun* (Targum Jonathan: “they will not be helped, and they will not be supported”).
And they will be carried off and abandoned, like the *shamir* and *shayit* of a vineyard; and beside the vineyard itself, in another place, it is translated *hovai u-vor*.
Isaiah.translator_note: The last clause is terse and its Aramaic left in transliteration.

Isaiah.english_translation: *Ve-al nevia afkid de-la yitnabun alehon* (Targum: “and upon the prophets I will charge that they not prophesy over them”). Prophecy is likened to rain, for the clouds receive it from the heavens; so the prophets receive prophecy from the mouth of the Holy.
Like *neta*; and because it is in the construct state, it is pointed (with a *patach*) like “the oxen for the sacrifice of peace-offerings” (Numbers 7:88).

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: And He looked for justice, but behold violence
Isaiah.english_translation: That they would do justice — and behold, *mispach*: an accumulation of sin upon sin, like “from cleaving” (*mi-hista-pe'ach*) (I Samuel 26). Another interpretation: an expression of plague. And because it is a wordplay in its reading, *mishpat* resembles *mispach*, and so *tze'akah* and *tzedakah*: the Holy Spirit fell upon it in the mouth of the prophet.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: Woe unto them that join house to house
Isaiah.english_translation: Twenty-two times “*ashrei*” is said in the Book of Psalms about those who uphold the Torah, and twenty-two times “*hoi*” did Isaiah say about the wicked. *Hoi* is an expression of a cry of sighing over the punishment destined to come.
They bring their houses near one another, and thereby rob the land of the weak poor who are between the two houses; and so:
“They bring field near to field, until there is no place” — for there is no place for a poor man to dwell.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: you be made to dwell Alone in the midst of the land
Isaiah.english_translation: You suppose that there is no portion for the Holy One, blessed be He, and none for the poor in the land. His portion in the tithes you rob, and the poor their land, so that you alone will dwell in it.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: In mine ears said the LORD of hosts
Isaiah.english_translation: The prophet said: My two ears heard when a decree was decreed upon them from the LORD, and with an oath: if it is not for this matter, many houses will be desolate, and great and good houses will be without inhabitant.

And because of the famine the inhabitants of the houses will go into exile, and there will be none dwelling in it. And this too will be measure for measure for you, for the bringing of field near to field, for you robbed the portion of the Omnipresent in the tithe of the land.
(*Arpent* in Old French.) And I say: as much as a day’s work with a yoke (*tzemed*) of cattle is called a *tzemed*.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is ארפינ״ט; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Arpents”) and reads *arpent*.

Isaiah.english_translation: One measure of wine, a *bat* of three *se'ah*.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: the seed of a homer shall yield an ephah
Isaiah.english_translation: A *beit kor*, which is thirty *se'ah* of grain, will yield an ephah of three *se'ah*.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: That tarry late into the night
Isaiah.english_translation: To drink wine at night.
Burning within them.
The *nevel* has more strings than the *kinnor*. And why is it called *nevel*? Because it disgraces (*menaveil*) all kinds of musical instruments — in Midrash Psalms.
It is of skin.
A flute of reed (*chalemiel* in Old French).
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is צלמיי״ל; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse, but the entry is badly garbled in my copy; the forms appear to be *chalemel* (a reed pipe). The reading is uncertain.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: they regard not the work of the LORD
Isaiah.english_translation: And in the Torah of the LORD they did not look (*u-ve-oraita de-HaShem lo istachalu*).

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: Neither have they considered the operation of His hands
Isaiah.english_translation: They made themselves as if they had not seen His mighty acts. Another interpretation: they did not praise Him in the morning, “Who forms light,” nor in the evening, “Who brings on the evenings.”
Because their heart was without knowledge.
His honourable ones will die in famine.
Thirsty, corresponding to the abundance of their drinking.
The Targum of *tzme'ah* (“thirsty”).
Measure for measure: they enlarged their desire to swallow food and drink in abundance and opened their mouths to swallow; so too Sheol will enlarge her desire to swallow.
And she opened.
Without end. And why “without measure” (*levli chok*)? Because these had no measure or limit in their delicacies.
The name of the splendour of Jerusalem.
Isaiah.translator_note: This short gloss is translated literally; its sense is not certain.

Isaiah.english_translation: The exultant ones in it.

*Ve-yechalash tokef gavrin* (“and the might of the strong men will be weakened”). And according to its Midrash, this is the Holy One, blessed be He, for they caused Him to appear like a stunned man, and so it says: “Of the Rock that begot thee thou wast unmindful” (Deuteronomy 32:18), and it says: “By slothfulness the rafters sink in” (Ecclesiastes 10:18).
When He executes judgments upon them, His name will be exalted in the world. “Through justice” — *jostise* in Old French.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is יושטיצ״א; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Justice”) and reads *jostise*.

Isaiah.english_translation: He will be sanctified among the righteous who remain among you.
Righteous ones who are likened to a flock of ewes.

According to their custom, in uprightness and in measure they conduct their affairs in judgment like these lambs. And our Rabbis expounded “*ke-dovram*” as “as it was spoken to them” — the consolations that were spoken to them.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: waste places of the fat ones
Isaiah.english_translation: The houses of the wicked, who are fat.
The righteous, who are as sojourners (*gerim*), will eat them.
Fat ones, like “I will offer unto Thee burnt-offerings of fatlings” (Psalms 66:15).

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: draw iniquity with cords of vanity
Isaiah.english_translation: They drag the evil inclination upon themselves little by little. At first it is “with cords of vanity,” like a thread of spider webs; and once it has been drawn upon them, it grows stronger and goes on until it becomes like the cart rope with which the carriage is tied, to draw.
A thing that has no substance.
*Chata'ah* — sin.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: Let Him make speed, let Him hasten His work
Isaiah.english_translation: The punishment that he says He will bring.
Whose word will stand.
They praise idolatry, and it is evil in their eyes to serve the Holy One, blessed be He, Who is good.
A thing that He is destined to bring darkness upon them — they say that it will give them light.
An iniquity for which He is destined to bring a bitter punishment upon them — they say that it will be sweet for them.
The service of the Holy One, blessed be He, which is sweet — they say that it is bitter.
To mix strong drink. The preparation of a drink is called *masakh*.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: take away the righteousness of the righteous from him
Isaiah.english_translation: Those who are worthy of acquittal in court, they remove from him, and hold him liable in judgment, and rob his money.
“And this thing will be for you,” etc.
As a tongue of fire eats the stubble.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: the chaff is consumed in the flame
Isaiah.english_translation: Jonathan translated: *amira* — straws of ears of grain; and like chaff that the flame loosens and makes into ashes.
Like a thing that rots (*nimok*).

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: their blossom shall go up as dust
Isaiah.english_translation: Their greatness is like dust that rises before a wind and departs; so it will depart.
On account of these deeds of theirs.
The kings of Judah and their princes.

Like spittle and vomit that is expelled from the body of a man, which is loathsome; and in the language of the Sages it is called *sachi*, and so “*sechi u-ma'os*” (Lamentations 3) [JPS: “offscouring and refuse”].

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: in the midst of the streets
Isaiah.english_translation: So will they be loathsome among the Babylonians.
That comes upon them.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: His anger is not turned away
Isaiah.english_translation: They did not amend their deeds so as to turn His anger away from them.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: His hand is stretched out still
Isaiah.english_translation: To do them harm.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: And He will lift up an ensign to the nations
Isaiah.english_translation: The Holy One, blessed be He, will lift up an ensign to the nations; He will hint hints to them to gather and come upon them. “Lifting up an ensign” is like a long pole (*kelones*), and they put a garment on its top and go up to the top of a high mountain and it is seen from afar, and it is a sign for the gathering of people; and so “I will set up My ensign to the peoples” (below 49), and so “and set it upon a pole” (Numbers 21:8). *Kelones* is *perche* in Old French; and because it is for a sign it is called *nes*.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is פירקא; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Un étendard : le mot hébreu signifie perche”) and reads *perche* (pole).

Isaiah.english_translation: *Sibler* in Old French; this too is a sign for gathering.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is שיבליר; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Il sifflera”) and reads *sibler* (*siffler*).

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: from the end of the earth
Isaiah.english_translation: That they will come from afar to besiege Israel.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: they shall come with speed swiftly
Isaiah.english_translation: The enemy upon them, as he goes on to explain.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: None shall be weary nor stumble among them
Isaiah.english_translation: He will not grow weary nor stumble in his running, to fulfil “Let Him make speed, let Him hasten” that they say before Him.
An expression of loosening, like “and he ungirded the camels” (Genesis 24:32).
And they will not see there any sign of failure, to be afraid of me from coming.
Isaiah.translator_note: The last phrase (לירא ממני מלבא) is translated literally; its sense is not certain.

Isaiah.english_translation: Targum Jonathan: *ke-tinra*, like *tzur*.
The wheels of his chariots.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: Their roaring shall be like a lion
Isaiah.english_translation: This terror will be upon you like a lion.
He will rescue it for his prey from the hand of all who come to rescue it. “*Yaflit*” — *esmocier* in Old French.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is אישקמוצייר; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Il saisira la proie”) with several manuscript forms of a word beginning *esmou-*; my transliteration of the printed form is approximate.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: roar against them in that day
Isaiah.english_translation: That enemy upon the people of the LORD mentioned above.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: Like the roaring of the sea
Isaiah.english_translation: As its waves roar, so will he come with roaring armies.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: if one look unto the land
Isaiah.english_translation: An expression of looking: Israel will look and hope that the kings of the earth, on whom they lean, will help them, as in the matter that is said: “that go down to Egypt for help” (below 31).
That there will be no one to help them. And *nabat* is a passive expression, like *lo niftach* and *lo nitak*; and the *vav* causes the speech to turn to the future: *iert esgardi* in Old French.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is אייר״ט איסגרד״י; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Et il sera regardé”) with several manuscript forms; I give the reading *iert esgardé*.

Isaiah.english_translation: Like “and he that helpeth shall stumble, and he that is helped shall fall” (there): the one who is in distress, upon whom the distress has come, and this one who came to give him light — both of them darkened. And some interpret: *tzar* is the moon, which has diminished, and *or* is the sun.
When its darkness comes — an expression of “My doctrine shall drop as the rain” (Deuteronomy 32); and so, in the manner of the dripping of rain, the light darkens.
Isaiah.translator_note:
The site’s JPS verse division places the clause “And the light is darkened in the skies thereof” at the start of 6:1, so the highlighted words here are only the nearest ones in 5:30.
u|The explanation is terse; translated literally.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: In the year that king Uzziah died
Isaiah.english_translation: When he was stricken with leprosy.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: and His train filled the temple
Isaiah.english_translation: Like “the skirts of the robe” (Exodus 28:34) — its bottom. I saw Him sitting on a throne in the heavens, and His feet in the Sanctuary — “the footstool of His feet” — in the Temple, to judge Uzziah, who came to take the crown of priesthood.
In the heavens.
To serve Him; so Jonathan translated: *shamshin kadishin be-ruma kadamohi* (“holy servants on high before Him”).

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: with twain he covered his face
Isaiah.english_translation: So that he not look toward the Shekhinah.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: with twain he covered his feet
Isaiah.english_translation: For modesty, so that his whole body not be seen before his Creator. And in Tanchuma: I saw the covering of the feet, because they are like the sole of a calf’s foot, so as not to remind Israel of the sin of the calf.
*U-ve-tarin meshamesh* (“and with two he serves”).

They take permission from one another, so that one not precede and begin and become liable to burning, unless they all open as one; and this is what [the poet] composed in *Yotzer Or*, in the Kedushah: “All of them answer as one,” etc. And Midrash Aggadah: it is the Work of the Chariot; and so Jonathan translated.
Three times, as its Targum.
*Eilot sippim* are the doorposts of the opening, which are measured in measures of cubits, in height and in width, and they are the doorposts of the Sanctuary.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: at the voice of them that called
Isaiah.english_translation: At the voice of the angels who call. And that was the day of the earthquake, of which it is said: “you shall flee, like as you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah” (Zechariah 14:5). On that day Uzziah stood to burn incense in the Sanctuary; the heavens quaked to burn him, to say that his sentence was burning, as it is said: “and devoured the two hundred and fifty men” (Numbers 16:35) — and this is why He called them *seraphim*, because they came to burn him. The earth quaked to swallow him, thinking that his sentence was to be swallowed up like Korah, who contended against the priesthood. A heavenly voice went out and said: “to be a memorial unto the children of Israel,” etc. (there), and that there should not be any more any man who disputes the priesthood, like Korah by swallowing and like his company by burning, but “as the LORD spoke by the hand of Moses” at the bush: “Put now thy hand into thy bosom” (Exodus 4:6), “and behold, his hand was leprous as snow”; so too here, leprosy broke out on his forehead.
Isaiah.translator_note: The printed “there” points to Numbers 16, but the words “to be a memorial unto the children of Israel” are Numbers 17:5, which is also the source of the phrase “as the LORD spoke by the hand of Moses.”

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: the house was filled with smoke
Isaiah.english_translation: It was filling with smoke.
Behold I am dying, for I was not worthy to see the face of the Shekhinah; and a parallel we find with Manoah: “We shall surely die, because we have seen God” (Judges 13:22).
Like “for all the people of Canaan are undone” (Zephaniah 1:11).
*De-mag'al be-chovin* (“who is defiled with sins”).

A coal; and so “*ugat ritzafim*” (I Kings 19:6) like *ugat reshafim*. And it is said in Isaiah and in Elijah with a *tzadi*, *ritzpah*, because they spoke slander (*delatoria*) about Israel: this one called them “a people of unclean lips,” and that one said “for they have forsaken Thy covenant” (there). The Holy One, blessed be He, said to the angel: Crush (*retzotz*) the mouth that spoke slander about My children.
Isaiah.translator_note: JPS renders 1 Kings 19:6 “a cake baked on the hot stones.”

Isaiah.english_translation: With tongs (*tzevat*).
That is in the Courtyard.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: and he touched my mouth with it
Isaiah.english_translation: “And thine iniquity is taken away” — from this, to chastise you, to atone for your iniquity for having reviled Israel. And great is its power, for the angel feared to take it except with tongs, and it touched the prophet’s lips and he was not harmed — in Tanchuma. And this is what is said: “for His camp is very great” (Joel 2:11) — these are the angels — “and mighty are those who do His word” (there) — they are the prophets. And Jonathan translated: *u-vi-dei ritzpah u-ve-fumeih memalel* (“and in his hand a coal, and in his mouth speaking”). The expression *ritzpah* is something fastened (*ratzuf*) in the mouth and on the tongue: he received the speech from the mouth of the Holy One, blessed be He, from His throne in the heavens, which was aligned opposite the altar that is in the Sanctuary.
Isaiah.translator_note: The Targum phrase is rendered as a translation of the Aramaic words as printed; the Aramaic is cited in transliteration.

Isaiah.english_translation: To rebuke Israel I sent Amos, and they used to call him *Pesilos* because he was heavy of tongue, and he prophesied two years before the earthquake; and Israel said: The Holy One, blessed be He, has abandoned the world, and has rested His Shekhinah upon this one with a cut-off tongue (*ha-din ketia lishna*), etc., as it is in the Pesikta.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: Hear you indeed, but understand not
Isaiah.english_translation: I am telling you “hear indeed,” and you do not set your heart to understand; “and see indeed” the miracles that I did for you, and you do not set your heart to know Me.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: Make the heart of this people fat
Isaiah.english_translation: Like “and he made heavy his heart” (Exodus 8:11). An expression of progress and of passive form: their heart goes on being made fat (*engraissant* in Old French), and their ears go on being made heavy from hearing.
Isaiah.translator_note:
Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is אנגריישנ״ט; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“S'engraisse”) and reads *engraissant*.
u|The grammatical phrase (לשון הלוך פעול) is terse; translated literally. JPS renders Exodus 8:11 “he hardened his heart.”

Isaiah.english_translation: Smeared, as in the matter that is said (below 44): “for their eyes are bedaubed, that they cannot see”; “the smeared (*ha-tuach*)” we translate *de-itsha*.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: Lest they, seeing with their eyes
Isaiah.english_translation: They set their heart not to hear the words of the prophets, for they fear lest his words be pleasing in their eyes and they understand in their heart and return to Me, and that is their healing.
How long will they make their hearts heavy and not hear?
I know that they will not return until the punishment comes upon them and they go into exile and their cities are desolate without inhabitant.
*Tisha'eh* — an expression of solitude (*galmud*), without inhabitant.
That the land will be forsaken of them; and this is the sense: forsaken places will be many in the midst of the land.

Even that remnant I will turn My hand against it, with refining after refining, and it will be for burning, until none remain except entirely righteous people, who will return to Me with all their heart.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: as a terebinth, and as an oak
Isaiah.english_translation: Which at the time of their casting (*shalechet*) shed their leaves in the days of autumn, shedding after shedding, until nothing is left in it except the trunk (*matzevet*); so too the holy seed that is found in it stand in its holiness; they will be a *matzevet* for it. Another interpretation: *matzevet* is its planting. Therefore I will not destroy them: I planted them, a holy seed. And some interpret: the Shalechet Gate was in Jerusalem, as it says in Ezra: “and there were terebinth and oak planted.”
Isaiah.translator_note: The quotation attributed here to Ezra is not matched in the book of Ezra (JPS), where I find no terebinth or oak; I translate as printed.

Isaiah.english_translation: Why did Scripture see fit to give his lineage? But because the end of the verse says “but could not prevail against it,” and it teaches you that the merit of the fathers stood for him. The ministering angels said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Woe (another version: Who) — who is this, that this wicked one reigns? He said to them: He is the son of Jotham, he is the son of Uzziah; his fathers were righteous; therefore I do not wish to stretch out My hand against him. That is what is said: “but could not prevail against it” — because of the merit of his fathers (in Bereshit Rabbah).

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: it was told the house of David
Isaiah.english_translation: Because he was wicked, He did not mention his name.

The king of Aram joined with the king of Israel to come upon you. *Nachah* is in the feminine form because the kingdom rested (*nachah*) — *poser* in Old French — an expression of “and rested in all the border of Egypt” (Exodus 6 [as printed]).
Isaiah.translator_note:
Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is פושי״ר; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Campe, se pose”) with several manuscript forms; the reading *poser* is offered as the sense, not a certain form.
The printed reference “Exodus 6” does not match; the words “and rested in all the border of Egypt” are in Exodus 10:14.

Isaiah.english_translation: Because each of them had already fought against him by himself and had overcome him, as it is said, “and the LORD his God delivered him into the hand of the king of Aram,” etc. (II Chronicles 28); it says, “and Pekah the son of Remaliah slew a hundred and twenty thousand men” — both in Chronicles (there).

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: as the trees of the forest are moved with the wind
Isaiah.english_translation: The sound of barren trees is heard more than of all fruit trees, as it is in Bereshit Rabbah.
A small remnant that will return to Me through you; and they are like your son.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: at the end of the conduit
Isaiah.english_translation: There you will find him. *Te'alat* (conduit) — *fossé* in Old French.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is פושי״ר; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Le fossé”) with manuscript forms such as *fosed* and פושיר and reads *fossé* (a ditch).

Isaiah.english_translation: Like a gathering of water that they make for fish.
On the slope of the mountain; and there is another pool lower than it, at its foot.

A field where the fullers spread out garments to dry them; so Jonathan translated. And our Rabbis expounded: Ahaz humbled himself before Isaiah, and put on his head the *okhla de-katzrei* — he covered himself with a vessel — that is, a perforated vessel of the fullers, with which they sprinkle water on garments.
Sit in peace, like wine on its lees.
They will be in your eyes as tails of firebrands whose flame has gone out. Firebrands (*udim*) — *tisons* in Old French.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is טיצונ״ש; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Tisons”) with manuscript forms such as טישונט; the reading is *tisons*.

Isaiah.english_translation: Let us rouse it with war.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: let us make a breach therein for us
Isaiah.english_translation: Let us make it level with us, like this valley (*bik'ah*), which is level; and so Targum Jonathan: *ve-nashvinun imana* — that they be equal with the ten tribes under one king.

“Son of the good for us” — so Targum Jonathan. And it can be explained: *tov El* that is not good in the eyes of the Omnipresent. And by the numerical substitution of the letters *albam*, *Tabeal* is *Remala*: *tet-resh*, *bet-mem*, *alef-lamed* — “son of Tabeal” is “son of Remala.”
Isaiah.translator_note: The expression *tov El* is translated as printed; its sense is not certain.

Isaiah.english_translation: This plan of theirs, that Judah would be subdued beneath them.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: the head of Aram is Damascus
Isaiah.english_translation: That is Damascus, and Jerusalem has nothing at all to do with them.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: the head of Damascus is Rezin
Isaiah.english_translation: The head will be in Damascus, and not in Jerusalem; and also Pekah and the ten tribes — within sixty-five years from the day that it was decreed in the days of Amos: “and Israel shall surely be led away captive out of his land” (Amos 7:11).

Ephraim will be crushed from being a people when Sennacherib exiles them together with their king Hoshea the son of Elah. Go and calculate from the prophecy of Amos until the ten tribes were exiled, and you will find them to be sixty-five years. The prophecy of Amos was two years before Uzziah was stricken, as is said (Amos 1:1): “two years before the earthquake”; and Uzziah was stricken twenty-five years — that makes twenty-seven; and the sixteen of Jotham, the sixteen of Ahaz, and the six of Hezekiah, as is said (II Kings 19 [as printed]): “and they took it, in the sixth year of Hezekiah, which was the ninth year of Hoshea,” “and carried Israel away unto Assyria” — that is sixty-five. And whence [do we know] that the days of Uzziah’s *chilufo* were twenty-five years? As is said (there, 15): “In the twenty and seventh year of Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel, Uzziah son of Amaziah began to reign over Judah.” Is it possible to say [so]? But did not Uzziah and Jeroboam reign together, by the reckoning that you will find in the Book of Kings? Rather, he reigned a stricken kingship: in the twenty-seventh year of his reign he was stricken, and he reigned fifty-two years. And it is impossible to count the sixty-five years from the day that Isaiah said this prophecy, for he said it in the days of Ahaz, and they were exiled in the sixth year of Hezekiah; and thus it is explained in Seder Olam, that Scripture counted from the prophecy of Amos.
Isaiah.translator_note:
The printed reference “II Kings 19” does not match: the words “in the sixth year of Hezekiah, which was the ninth year of Hoshea” are at II Kings 18:10 and “and carried Israel away unto Assyria” at II Kings 17:6. The verse at II Kings 15:1 reads “Azariah” (JPS), not “Uzziah.”
u|The sentence beginning “Is it possible to say” is terse in the printed text; translated literally. The word *chilufo* is left in transliteration.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: If you will not have faith
Isaiah.english_translation: In my prophecy, you, Ahaz and his people, for I know that you are wicked.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: surely you shall not be established
Isaiah.english_translation: There is no faith in you.
*Ve-osif nevia de-HaShem* (“and the prophet of the LORD added”).
For this thing, because I know that you do not believe the words of the Holy One, blessed be He.

Make deep and ask a request — like “hear” (*shema'ah*), “forgive” (*selachah*) (Daniel 9:19): ask a sign in the depths of the abyss, to bring a dead man back to life for you; or make it high above, to ask a sign in the heavens.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: neither will I try the LORD
Isaiah.english_translation: It is not my wish that His name be sanctified through me.
The prophets of the LORD.
Because He knows that you do not believe in Him, and you have wearied Him with your wickedness.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: the Lord Himself shall give you a sign
Isaiah.english_translation: He Himself will give, of His own accord, against your will.

It is a future expression, as we find with the wife of Manoah, to whom the angel said: “and thou shalt conceive, and bear a son” (Judges 13:3), and it is written: “And he said to her: ‘lo, thou shalt conceive’ [*harah*]” (Judges 13:5), etc.
My wife is with child this year, and that was the fourth year of Ahaz.
The Holy Spirit will rest upon her.

To say that our Rock will be with us. And this is the sign: for she is a young woman and had never prophesied, and the Holy Spirit will rest upon this one; and this is what is said below: “And I went unto the prophetess,” etc. And we do not find the wife of a prophet called a prophetess unless she prophesied. And some interpret that it was said about Hezekiah, but it is impossible, for when you count his years you will find that Hezekiah was born nine years before his father’s reign. And some interpret: this is the sign, that she was a young woman and not fit to bear a child.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: Curd and honey shall he eat
Isaiah.english_translation: The child — that our land will be full of every good.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: when he knoweth to refuse the evil, and choose the good
Isaiah.english_translation: When he knows to refuse the evil and choose the good; and from where do we have this good? Is not the land now laid waste by the troops of the kings of the land and of Pekah the son of Remaliah?

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: the land whose two kings thou hast a horror of shall be forsaken
Isaiah.english_translation: The land will be forsaken by its inhabitants: the land of Rezin and the land of Pekah.

And be in dread because of its two kings, Rezin and Pekah; for in that year the king of Assyria went up against Damascus, because Ahaz had hired him, as it is said in the Book of Kings (II Kings 16): “and took it, and carried the people of it captive to Kir, and slew Rezin.” And in that same year, “And Hoshea the son of Elah made a conspiracy against Pekah the son of Remaliah, and smote him, and slew him,” in the twentieth year of Jotham (there 15), which is the fourth year of Ahaz.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: The LORD shall bring upon thee, and upon thy people
Isaiah.english_translation: Upon Hezekiah your son, who will reign after you; and because he is righteous, He did not call him his son.
Isaiah.translator_note: The pronoun “his” in the last clause is ambiguous in the printed text (whose son); translated literally.

Isaiah.english_translation: From the day that the kingdom of the house of David was divided and Ephraim departed from Judah. And what are these days? The days of the host of the king of Assyria; and even in them he did [this] to Judah. And so we count (II Chronicles 28:20) that he came at first upon Ahaz, as it is written: “And Tillegath-pilneser king of Assyria came unto him, and distressed him, but strengthened him not”; and in the days of Hezekiah his son the miracle was done.
He will hint to them that they gather.
Many armies, like flies, from the land of Egypt will come with Sennacherib.
Because all the land of Egypt is made of rivers (*ye'orim*), for the rains do not fall there, but the Nile rises and waters it.
An army of mighty men who sting like bees.
Valleys of depths, uncultivated fields.
To lie in ambush; *nekikei* — the clefts of the rock.
The place of the briers (*sirim*), which are called *broces* in Old French; and so “instead of the thorn shall come up the cypress” (below 55).
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is ברוצ״ש; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“Des broussailles”) and reads *broces* (modern *brousses*).

Isaiah.english_translation: *Batei toshavachta* (“houses of praise”).
Isaiah.translator_note: The Aramaic phrase is translated literally; its sense as an explanation of this word is not certain.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: shave with a razor that is hired
Isaiah.english_translation: The great one; and so “also her hired men in the midst of her” (Jeremiah 46:21); Targum Jonathan: *rabrevaha yegalach* (“her great ones he will shave”).

By those who dwell beyond the River; and with whom? With those who dwell with the king of Assyria. “The head” he will shave, and “the hair of the feet” — because it is in the construct state, it changed to be pointed with a *patach*.
Isaiah.translator_note: The words “and with whom” are translated literally from the printed text and may be corrupt.

Isaiah.english_translation: It will finish. And the shaving is the killing, and the razor is the sword.
He is Sennacherib.
*Mashrayteih* (“his camps”).
*Shaltoniya* (“rulers”). And our Rabbis said: it is actual shaving, and the sweeping away of the beard is its burning with fire — the beard of Sennacherib, as it is in Aggadat Chelek.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: a man shall rear a young cow, and two sheep
Isaiah.english_translation: And because their land will be empty, since the armies will plunder the animals, with the little that remains I will give blessing.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: for the abundance of milk that they shall give
Isaiah.english_translation: The milk that these two sheep will make — they will despise the milk, and will eat the curd, which is the fat of the milk.
The righteous who escape the sword of Sennacherib: He announces to them good tidings, that sustenance will come to them after all that desolation.
That the land will be desolate; it will be the place where they were before the armies came.
Isaiah.translator_note: The printed sentence is terse and possibly corrupt; translated literally.

Isaiah.english_translation: Worth a thousand pieces of silver, they will be for briers and thorns, for their owners will leave them and flee; and they bring up nettles (*kimshonim*), and worms, and scorpions.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: With arrows and with bow shall one come thither
Isaiah.english_translation: Whoever wants to enter into it will need a bow and arrows in his hand, to save himself from wild beasts and snakes and scorpions.
Where there are white fields for grain.
It is a kind of hoe, which is called *fossoir* in Old French.
Isaiah.translator_note: Old French gloss: the printed Hebrew spelling is פשויי״ר; Darmesteter (1909) lists this verse (“La bêche”) with forms such as פוטוייר and reads *fosoir* (a spade).

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: thou shalt not come thither for fear of briers and thorns
Isaiah.english_translation: For in them they will busy themselves with sowing grain for food, for it is impossible without grain; but the vines will be for plunder. For that generation of Hezekiah will return to Me to engage in Torah and not to drink wine; and so it was, as is in [tractate Sanhedrin] Chelek: they searched from Dan to Beersheba and did not find a man who was not expert in the laws of the forbidden and the permitted, and the unclean and the clean. And about that generation it says, “and it shall come to pass … every place,” etc.; this is what is said (Proverbs 25:1): “which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out.”

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: for the sending forth of oxen
Isaiah.english_translation: There their cattle will graze on fat pasture.
A scroll.
In a script that any man who reads in it can read, even the least of men, even one who is not wise; and so Targum Jonathan: *ketav mefarash* (“an explicit writing”).

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: The spoil speedeth, the prey hasteth
Isaiah.english_translation: For Sennacherib to come and plunder all the wealth of the ten tribes, and for Nebuchadnezzar after him to hasten to spoil Zedekiah and his generation.

Also in those days, the days of Jehoiakim, concerning that punishment: two faithful witnesses — the one to announce to them the evil that was to come upon them: Uriah the priest, whom Jehoiakim killed, as it is said (Jeremiah 26:20): “And there was also a man that prophesied in the name of the LORD, Uriah the son of Shemaiah of Kiriath-jearim; and he prophesied against this city and against this place all the words of Jeremiah.”
Isaiah.translator_note: Rashi’s wording of Jeremiah 26:20 differs slightly from the JPS verse (“against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah”); translated as printed.

Isaiah.english_translation: “In the second year of Darius”: “There shall yet old men and old women sit in the broad places of Jerusalem” (Zechariah 8:4). Uriah is a sign for Zechariah: if you see that the prophecy of Uriah is fulfilled, you will be expecting that the prophecy of Zechariah will be fulfilled; just as He made witnesses concerning Sennacherib, Amos and Isaiah — Amos for the punishment of the ten tribes, “and Israel shall surely be led away captive” (Amos 7:11), and Isaiah (below 32) for the promise to Hezekiah when he would reign.

He is the very son whom the prophetess called Immanuel, because the Holy One, blessed be He, was a help to Hezekiah when he would reign. And it is impossible to say that he is a second son, for we have learned that this prophecy was said in the fourth year of Ahaz, and in the fourth year of Ahaz Pekah was slain, and it is impossible for two sons to be born in one year, one after the other. And Isaiah his father called his name Maher-shalal [-hashbaz] on account of the punishment destined to come upon Rezin and the son of Remaliah, who were coming to take the kingship from the house of David and the cessation of the kingship of Hezekiah.
“And he went up to Damascus and took it” (II Kings 16).

After Pekah was slain and Hoshea reigned in his place, Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up, and Hoshea became his servant, and gave him a gift and a bribe (there, 16) — that is the spoil of Samaria. All this was in the fourth year of Ahaz.
Isaiah.translator_note: The printed reference is “there, 16”; the words “and Hoshea became his servant” are at II Kings 17:3 (JPS: “and brought him presents”), and “a present” sent by Ahaz is II Kings 16:8.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: The waters of Shiloah that go softly
Isaiah.english_translation: In the kingdom of the house of David, which leads them gently, like the waters of Shiloach that flow gently (*be-malkhuta de-veit David de-madbar lehon be-nicha ke-mei Shiloacha de-nagdin be-nicha*). Shiloach is a spring, and its name is Gihon and Shiloach. For they wished to remove the kingdom of the house of David in the days of Ahaz, for Pekah the son of Remaliah; and here he prophesied about Shebna and his company, who wished to rebel against Hezekiah, whom they despised because they saw that he did not choose the table of kings but ate a *litra* of vegetables and engaged in Torah — about him it is said, “The righteous eateth to the satisfying of his desire” (Proverbs 13:25). And they saw Pekah the son of Remaliah eating forty *se'ah* of fledglings as a dessert after the meal, and they used to mock Hezekiah and say: Is this one fit to be king? This is not a king, but Rezin and the son of Remaliah were fit to reign in their lifetimes — and this is “and rejoiceth with Rezin,” etc. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them: You are eaters, you desire [to eat]; I will bring upon you many eaters: “Behold, the Lord bringeth up upon them,” etc., “the waters of the River, mighty” — in place of the waters of Shiloah, weak and gentle.
The River.
His waters will grow strong to rise over all the channels where his waters issue.
The river fills over all its banks; “on his banks” (*gedodav*) means its steep lips, in the place where the river draws between steep embankments, and it is as if inside a gutter.
In the land of Judah.
With force.
To the main strength of their neck; and Targum Jonathan: *ad Yerushalem yimta* (“to Jerusalem he will reach”).

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: the stretching out of his wings
Isaiah.english_translation: The small segment at the end of the wing is called *moto*; and I saw in Tanchuma: how large are the *motot* of a rooster’s wings? One of sixty compared to the multitude of Sennacherib.
The land of Judah.
It is the tribe of Judah, to whom the Holy One, blessed be He, promised to be with them in the days of Hezekiah, in accordance with the word of the prophetess who called her son’s name Immanuel.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: Make an uproar, O you peoples
Isaiah.english_translation: An expression of *re'ehu*, *re'echa* (his companion, your companion). From a manuscript: *itchabaru* (“they joined together”) — the multitude of Sennacherib joined together.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: you shall be broken in pieces
Isaiah.english_translation: And you shall be broken.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: Gird yourselves, and you shall be broken in pieces
Isaiah.english_translation: Gird yourselves with all kinds of might — and your end will be to be broken.
An expression of command.

When the prophecy grew strong upon me, when He added to speak to me about this matter, as it is written above, “And the LORD spoke again unto me” (above 7); and in this language it says (Ezekiel 17 [as printed]): “and the hand of the LORD was strong upon me” — an expression of prophecy.
Isaiah.translator_note: The words quoted from “above 7” are Isaiah 7:10, which reads “spoke again unto Ahaz”; the Ezekiel quotation (“and the hand of the LORD was strong upon me”) is Ezekiel 3:14, not chapter 17.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: admonishing me that I should not walk in the way of this people
Isaiah.english_translation: He warned me not to be in the counsel of Shebna the scribe and his company, who conspired to rebel against Hezekiah, as is explained (in Sanhedrin 26 [as printed]); and there is an allusion in this book (below 22): “Go, get thee unto this steward,” etc.
Like *ve-lyasreni*.
You, the company of Hezekiah, even though you are fewer than the company of Shebna, do not say: “after the many to pervert [justice].”
Isaiah.translator_note: The wording is that of Exodus 23:2 (JPS: “after a multitude to pervert justice”).

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: concerning all whereof this people do say: A conspiracy
Isaiah.english_translation: That the people of Shebna — because it is a conspiracy of wicked men and is not to be counted; and so with the conspiracy of the ten tribes, who conspired with the kings of Egypt.
This people, who say to you to fear Sennacherib and to make peace with him.
Do not say, “He is strong”; so Targum Jonathan: *la timrun takif*.
He who strengthens you.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: And He shall be for a sanctuary
Isaiah.english_translation: That counsel which Shebna counseled and which Pekah counseled, to put an end to the kingship of the house of David, will be a sign of punishment to come upon them.
Like “Sanctify yourselves for tomorrow” (Joshua 3).
For the feet are struck (*nigafim*) on them; an expression of stumbling, like “before your feet stumble” (Jeremiah 13:16), “lest thou dash thy foot against a stone” (Psalms 91:12).
It is the same as “stone of stumbling,” for a *tzur* is a stone.
Who came to be a gin and a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And who are the two houses? Pekah the son of Remaliah and his company, and Shebna and his company.

Isaiah.english_lemma_JPS: And many among them shall stumble
Isaiah.english_translation: And those stones — these and their companies will stumble; both will fall into the hands of their enemies: Pekah was killed (Hoshea killed him), and the ten tribes fell into the hand of Sennacherib, and Shebna went out from Jerusalem when Sennacherib went up from it to go against Tirhakah king of Cush; Shebna and his company were swept away, and he went on his way.
Isaiah.translator_note: The last clause (שטף שבנא וסיעתו והלך לו) is translated literally; the subject is not certain.
